data.name: Neverwinter Nights: Enhanced Edition
data.detailed_description:
Neverwinter Nights: Enhanced Edition adds all-new enhanced features to the content of Neverwinter Nights Diamond Edition.

Slink through the shadows as a deadly half-elven rogue, wield fearsome magics as a powerful gnomish sorcerer, vanquish your foes as an armor-clad dwarven paladin... whatever hero you create, incredible adventures await.

Discover magic, wonder, and danger at every turn on your own or with friends in these classic Dungeons & Dragons adventures.

Enhanced Features:

  • Improved Display: Your portrait, combat bar, inventory, and other UI elements adjust in size based on your chosen resolution including 1080p and 4k.
  • Advanced Graphics Options: Pixel shaders and post-processing effects make for crisper, cleaner visuals. Enable contrast, vibrance, and depth of field options as preferred.
  • Community Endorsed: Original developers have teamed with key members of the Neverwinter Nights community to curate important fan-requested improvements to support players, storytellers, and modders.
  • Backwards Compatibility: Works with save games, modules, and mods from the original Neverwinter Nights. A galaxy of community created content awaits.
  • Restored Multiplayer: A completely rebuilt multiplayer system makes it easy to find online persistent worlds and game with friends
  • More Modder Opportunities: Toolset quality-of-life improvements, shaders, filters, texture maps, and a new material systems allow creators to make amazing looking models and modules.

All the content of Neverwinter Nights Diamond Edition:

The original Neverwinter Nights campaign: Find yourself at the center of intrigue, betrayal, and dark magic in Neverwinter Nights. Journey through dangerous cities, monster filled dungeons and deep into uncharted wilderness in search of the cure for a cursed plague ravaging the city of Neverwinter.
Two expansion packs:
  • Shadows of Undrentide: Another adventure begins in Shadows of Undrentide! Charged by your master to recover four ancient artifacts, travel from the Silver Marches to unravel mysteries of a long-dead magical civilization.
  • Hordes of the Underdark: Continue the adventure started in Shadows of Undrentide and journey into the ever-more bizarre and hostile depths of Undermountain to challenge a gathering evil.
Three premium modules:
Discover over 40 hours of new stories, then go on to sample the hundreds of modules created by community members just like you.
  • Kingmaker
  • ShadowGuard
  • Witch’s Wake
The Aurora Toolset: Build your own world full of unique monsters, items, traps, encounters, and settings, then share your creation with the rest of the Neverwinter Nights community. (Windows only)
Dungeon Master Client: Become the storyteller! Control monsters, creatures, and characters your players will meet over the course of an adventure.

reviews.review:
tl;dr
RIP BioWare. Baldur’s Gate demonstrated your storytelling, Dragon Age showed off your worldbuilding, and Mass Effect & KotOR brought Western RPGs to consoles and a wider audience. But Neverwinter Nights was a unique offering I don't think any studio has replicated.

NWN is an extraordinary D&D storytelling platform that happens to ship with perfectly OK campaigns. Few games match its easy-to-use yet powerful toolset, persistent online worlds and thriving community. Twenty years of free, player-made modules are hard to beat for value. 

A strong recommendation for RPG fans, just don't expect the official campaign to be the main event.

Player context
Played the original boxed game in the early 2000s, never touched Diamond Edition. This is my first replay since then. Linux native build (no issues), single-player only so I can't speak to the current state of online play. Beyond modern resolutions, new graphical options (maxxing everything will slow down game considerably) and Steam Workshop integration, the game seems largely unchanged from memory. Understandable, as breaking compatibility with 20 years of fan-made modules and saves would be meshuggah.

The campaigns
Baldur’s Gate, Icewind Dale and Fallout made me love RPGs as a child, and NWN looked then set to surpass them with 3D graphics, 3E rules and freer character building. Instead, the original campaign (Wailing Death) left me cold. I barely remembered anyone beyond Aribeth and Desther, whose arcs are telegraphed a mile away, and nothing made Neverwinter feel as alive as Amn did in BG2. The structure is painfully obvious: a central hub surrounded by zones where you collect plot MacGuffins to progress to the next chapter, then repeat. To every problem encountered, the solution was almost always go here and kill thing. It reads like a campaign built after the toolset and multiplayer were the priority (it was). Replaying it now, it wasn't as bad as I remembered, just passable. Newcomers may find the tutorial useful, but won't lose much by skipping to SoU.

Shadows of Undrentide was much more the single-player RPG I'd originally wanted: tighter, with better low-level progression, more reactive NPCs, and companions whose levelling and gear you control.

Hordes of the Underdark went further with storytelling, stronger companions, professional voice acting, satisfying epic-level play and new areas. I may have been more excited by the prestige classes and epic levels than the campaign itself at the time, however. The Cania sections felt like a slog in places. It's also the buggiest of the three: dismissed companions can vanish permanently, and a bugged cutscene cost me Mephisto plot points.

My suggested order is SoU first, then import your character into HotU. Wailing Death is for completionists only.

Beyond the official campaigns
Once you've finished them, there's a whole other game waiting. Darkness Over Daggerford and Tyrants of the Moonsea are excellent premium modules (separate paid DLC, so check their own Steam reviews), while the same author's Siege of Shadowdale and Crimson Tides of Tethyr are free. The EE also signposts curated community campaigns like Eye of the Beholder, the Auren sagas and Cult of the Reptile God. Quality control is less consistent than in commercial releases (typos, awkward maps, weird bugs and pacing), but you get immersive adventures in lesser-known corners of the Forgotten Realms, or entirely original settings.

Beyond the Workshop is Neverwinter Vault, with modules refined over nearly twenty years. Want a brutal test of your build? Swordflight. Prefer an ambitious, story-driven adventure? The Prophet series. The Aielund Saga and A Hunt Through the Dark are good places to start exploring. I played online back in the day, and it's lovely seeing worlds I remember still apparently going strong.

The good
Modules (free or premium) are NWN's biggest strength, showing the engine can support far better adventures than the original campaign suggests.

Thanks to the 3E rules, this is one of the best games for building a D&D character and watching the build express itself, with more flexibility than the Infinity Engine's AD&D rules.

When module makers make good use of the sound design, it's superb: hymns from an Umberlee temple drifting down into the sewers, a floorboard creaking over a hidden stash. Responsiveness to player actions is at the heart of great games, and this is especially true of RPGs.

Back in 2002, the game was considered a looker with its 512x512 textures. Obviously primitive by standards today, but I feel it has aged well. NWN2 wowed me graphically back then, but NWN's cleaner more readable style has aged better in my opinion.

The bad
Original campaign quests too often boil down to an NPC sending you somewhere to kill things, collect an object and return. I'd rather investigate, decide and choose a resolution. SoU and HotU sometimes offer that, but Wailing Death doesn't.

The interface is dated. People complained about how lacking in character it could feel back then, still true today. The dialogue box sits in a corner instead of the centre or bottom of the screen like 99% of other RPGs. This was more defensible at 1024x768 in 2003 when it took a quarter of the screen, but it's awkwardly tiny at modern resolutions or broken when scaled up.

Character-based saves would help, especially when you have only one quicksave and one autosave slot.

Resting, lockpicking and trap-disarming all need timers, so with so many locks and traps you spend ages watching progress bars. I assume the original intention was to make thieving tense, with guards potentially walking around the corner and spotting you breaking into a treasury, but that gameplay was never really implemented. Some modules remove the pointless rest timer.

Many bugs remain after all these years: moonwalking characters, inventory breaking if you change equipment mid-combat, dead NPCs that spawn and flop over as you approach. I distinctly remember all this from 2003, and it's still in the game today.

No dwarf mohawk hair option, so no going full Gotrek in this game :(

The ugly
NWN's companions follow a different philosophy from BG2's, but they're still the weakest part of the single-player game. They're mostly just bodies to throw at enemies or traps, lockpickers, and loot mules. There's no meaningful target prioritisation or direct control. Spellcasters waste spells on low-level enemies and summons instead of the summoners, on open maps companions aggro distant enemies and drag whole areas into combat. Defend, Follow and Attack commands feel like suggestions. They get stuck in doorways, and their pathfinding is still dogshit after all this time, especially when you're hasted and they're half a map behind.

Managing their gear is busywork, too. Right-click, More Actions, Inventory, then open your own inventory to move items, with only one companion inventory or character sheet open at a time. I prefer playing solo; spells, gear, magic bags and builds that cover most of what companions offer, minus the hassle.

Conclusion
Don't treat NWN as a successor to the Infinity Engine games. It was trying to be something different by being a character-building sandbox, rules playground, multiplayer/DM platform, adventure toolset and home to excellent campaigns. The original campaign was never a great demonstration, but the expansions and community content show why this deserves its reputation today and played rather than just admired.

Tips for newcomers
Parry skill and feats are worse than useless, so are Initiative feats. Ignore them.

Hit locked doors or cast damaging spells on them; no need for a rogue or learn their skills.

Strength beats Dexterity for melee, with their boosts being easier to find.

Clerics are overpowered. Self-buffed melee clerics make great frontliners and summoners, ideal for a first playthrough.

Save manually occasionally. You only have one quicksave and autosave slot each.
